query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) interlayer, developed through a controlled composition change strategy, will mitigate the thermal expansion mismatch and suppress interdiffusion between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr, thereby enhancing interfacial stability under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W and CuCrZr substrates as used in current reactor designs, with known issues of interfacial stresses and diffusion when directly bonded.
generation.intervention: Introduce an RHEA interlayer—engineered through composition change and optimized via diffusion bonding experiments—to serve as a transitional layer between W and CuCrZr.
generation.conditions: Simulated fusion reactor environments including high temperatures, high heat flux, thermal cycling, and operation under inert atmosphere or high vacuum.
generation.structural_mediator: The tailored grain structure and intermediate thermal expansion coefficient of the RHEA interlayer create a graded interface that accommodates the mismatch in properties between W and CuCrZr.
generation.mechanism: The RHEA interlayer reduces interdiffusion by serving as an effective diffusion barrier thanks to its low atomic diffusivity, while its intermediate thermal expansion properties lessen mechanical stresses and inhibit the formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in interdiffusion and thermal stress at the interface, leading to improved mechanical integrity and longer-term stability of the bonded W/CuCrZr structure under extreme fusion reactor conditions.
generation.baseline: Direct bonding of W and CuCrZr commonly leads to pronounced interdiffusion and high interfacial stresses due to mismatches in thermal expansion and diffusion behavior.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the RHEA interlayer is expected under conditions typical of fusion reactor operations; however, its performance may be limited if extreme irradiation effects or unforeseen chemical interactions predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in interdiffusion suppression and thermal stress reduction require further experimental calibration, and the long-term irradiation behavior of the interlayer remains to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W/CuCrZr joints—one with the engineered RHEA interlayer and one without. Subject both to simulated fusion reactor conditions (high temperature, thermal cycling, high heat flux under inert atmosphere or vacuum) using diffusion bonding methods. Employ SEM and EDS to characterize the interfacial microstructures and measure interdiffusion depths.
measurements: Elemental distribution and interdiffusion profiles using EDS
Residual thermal stresses measured by appropriate techniques (e.g., X-ray diffraction)
Mechanical performance tests (e.g., shear strength) of the bonded joints
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the joints with the RHEA interlayer do not show significantly reduced interdiffusion, lower residual thermal stresses, and improved mechanical performance compared to the directly bonded W/CuCrZr baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations
